title: What are the database lock types: Shared (S, read, many allowed concurrently), Exclusive (X, write, only one), and Intent locks (signal an intention to lock at a lower granularity so the engine can check compatibility cheaply): and what is lock escalation (the engine converting many fine-grained row locks into fewer coarse-grained table/page locks to reduce overhead, at the cost of concurrency)?
shortTitle: Database Lock Types (Shared, Exclusive, Intent) and Lock Escalation

s1_definition.oneliner: Shared locks allow many concurrent readers, Exclusive locks allow one writer, Intent locks signal fine-grained locking for cheap compatibility checks, and lock escalation trades many row locks for a coarse table lock to cut overhead at the cost of concurrency.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Shared lock (S)** – acquired to read a resource; multiple transactions can hold it concurrently, but it is incompatible with an Exclusive lock.
- **Exclusive lock (X)** – acquired to modify a resource; only one transaction can hold it, blocking all other access.
- **Intent locks (IS/IX)** – placed on a coarser level (table) to signal that a finer-grained lock (row) exists below, letting the engine check compatibility in O(1) without scanning every row lock.
- **Lock escalation** – the engine automatically converts many fine-grained row locks into a single coarse table lock when the count exceeds a threshold (around 5000 in SQL Server), reducing overhead but blocking unrelated transactions.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India's ledger. A shared lock is many auditors reading the same page together: allowed, since reading does not conflict. An exclusive lock is one clerk editing a line while everyone else waits. An intent lock is a note on the cover saying "someone inside is editing a line," so another person wanting to lock the whole ledger can see the conflict instantly. Lock escalation is when so many individual lines are locked that the librarian just locks the whole ledger: less bookkeeping, but nobody else can touch any line.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Database locks coordinate concurrent access, and the three types to know are shared, exclusive, and intent locks. A Shared lock is taken to read a resource and is compatible with other shared locks, so many transactions can read the same row at once. An Exclusive lock is taken to modify a resource and is incompatible with everything, so only one transaction holds it and all other access waits.

Intent locks are placed at a coarser level like a table before a transaction takes a finer lock on a row beneath it. Their purpose is pure efficiency: they are a cheap flag that lets the engine detect a conflict with a table-level request in constant time instead of scanning thousands of individual row locks.

Lock escalation is the engine automatically converting many fine-grained locks into one coarse-grained lock when a transaction accumulates too many of them. SQL Server escalates around five thousand locks by replacing the row locks with a single table lock. This slashes bookkeeping cost, but the trade-off is concurrency: a table-level exclusive lock blocks every other transaction. At the National Bank of India a year-end job that updated an interest flag on millions of accounts caused exactly this, and the fix was batching the update into small chunks.

Remember one sentence: Shared locks allow many readers, Exclusive locks allow one writer, Intent locks cheaply signal fine-grained locking for fast compatibility checks, and lock escalation trades many row locks for a coarse table lock.

---

keyPoints: A Shared lock (S) is for reading and is compatible with other S locks; multiple readers coexist.
An Exclusive lock (X) is for writing and blocks all other access including readers.
Intent locks (IS, IX) are placed at the table level to signal row-level locks below, enabling O(1) compatibility checks.
Lock escalation converts many row locks into a table lock when the count exceeds a threshold (around 5000 in SQL Server).
Escalation reduces overhead but blocks unrelated transactions on the same table.
Batch large updates into chunks to avoid escalation and keep other transactions unblocked.
InnoDB and PostgreSQL use row-level locking with MVCC and do not escalate the way SQL Server does.
